cards.back: The kinetic energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, equal to 1.60 x 10^-19 J.

keyPoints.text: kinetic energy gained by an electron
accelerated through a potential difference of one volt

cards.explanation: It is an energy, not a voltage: eV = (1.60 x 10^-19 C) x 1 V = 1.60 x 10^-19 J.

cards.back: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of high enough frequency falls on it.
cards.explanation: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted at all, however bright the source, which a wave model cannot explain.

cards.front: Define the work function of a metal.
cards.back: The minimum energy needed to release an electron from the surface of that metal.

keyPoints.text: release an electron from the surface

cards.explanation: Electrons deeper in the metal need more energy than this, so the work function sets the threshold frequency through hf = phi.

synonyms: photon energy equals work function plus KE max

cards.explanation: One photon gives all of its energy hf to one electron; the work function pays for the escape and whatever is left becomes the electron's kinetic energy.

cards.front: Why does the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons not increase when the radiation is made brighter?
cards.back: Because each electron absorbs one photon. Increasing intensity increases the number of photons per second and so the number of electrons released, but each photon still carries the same energy hf.

keyPoints.text: one photon is absorbed by one electron

synonyms: energy per photon stays the same

keyPoints.text: intensity changes the number of photons

cards.explanation: This is the observation that forced the particle model of light: a wave model predicts that a brighter source would eventually give electrons more energy.

cards.front: Calculate the energy of a photon of green light of wavelength 550 nm, in joules and in electronvolts.

synonyms: use the wavelength form of the photon energy

cards.explanation: $E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{550 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.62 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. Dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ gives $2.26\,\mathrm{eV}$. Visible photons are of order a few electronvolts, which is a scale worth having in mind: it is why the electronvolt is the natural unit for atomic transitions and why a joule is an absurdly large one.

cards.front: A metal has a work function of $3.0 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. Calculate its threshold frequency.

keyPoints.text: threshold frequency is when the photon energy just equals the work function

synonyms: divide the work function by Planck's constant

cards.explanation: At the threshold the emitted electron has zero kinetic energy, so $hf_0 = \phi$ and $f_0 = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}} = 4.52 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Below this frequency no electrons are emitted at all, however intense the light - the observation that classical wave theory cannot explain, and the reason Einstein's photon model was needed.

cards.front: Radiation of frequency $1.0 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ falls on a metal of work function $3.0 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

keyPoints.text: hf = work function + maximum kinetic energy
subtract the work function to get 3.63 x 10^-19 J

cards.explanation: $hf = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 10^{15} = 6.63 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, and subtracting the work function gives $3.63 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, or about $2.3\,\mathrm{eV}$. This is the maximum, not the typical value: electrons from below the surface lose energy on the way out, so only those at the very surface emerge with the full amount.

cards.front: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at $2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
cards.explanation: $p = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 2.0 \times 10^{6} = 1.82 \times 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, so $\lambda = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{1.82 \times 10^{-24}} = 3.64 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$. That this is the same order as the spacing between atoms in a crystal is exactly why electron diffraction works, and why an electron microscope resolves far finer detail than a light one.

cards.front: How do an emission line spectrum and an absorption line spectrum of the same element differ, and what produces each?
cards.back: Emission is bright lines on a dark background, produced when electrons fall between levels and emit photons. Absorption is dark lines on a continuous background, produced when electrons absorb photons of exactly those energies.

keyPoints.text: emission: bright lines on a dark background
absorption: dark lines on a continuous spectrum
electrons falling produce emission and rising produce absorption
the lines appear at the same wavelengths

mcq.correct: Bright lines from falling electrons; dark lines where photons are absorbed, at the same wavelengths
distractors: Dark lines from falling electrons; bright lines where photons are absorbed
Emission is continuous and absorption is a line spectrum
They are the same pattern, differing only in brightness

cards.explanation: The lines coincide because the same energy differences are involved, just traversed in opposite directions. Absorption lines appear only for transitions starting from populated levels, which at ordinary temperatures means the ground state, so an absorption spectrum usually shows fewer lines than the emission spectrum of the same element.

cards.front: An electron falls between levels of $-1.5\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $-3.4\,\mathrm{eV}$. Find the energy of the photon emitted, in joules.

keyPoints.text: the photon energy is the difference between the levels

cards.explanation: The energy difference is $3.4 - 1.5 = 1.9\,\mathrm{eV}$, and $1.9 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 3.04 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$. Level energies are negative because they are measured from the ionisation level at zero, so subtracting two negatives gives a positive photon energy. The second distractor adds the magnitudes instead of taking the difference.

cards.front: State two observations of the photoelectric effect that a classical wave model of light cannot explain.
cards.back: That no electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency however intense the light, and that the maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency rather than intensity. Emission is also instantaneous.

keyPoints.text: no emission below a threshold frequency
synonyms: intensity cannot compensate for low frequency

keyPoints.text: maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity
synonyms: brighter light does not give faster electrons

mcq.correct: Threshold frequency, and kinetic energy depending on frequency not intensity
distractors: Emission depends on intensity, and there is a measurable delay
Electrons are emitted at all frequencies, and energy depends on intensity
The number of electrons depends on frequency, and their energy on intensity

cards.explanation: Classically, energy arrives continuously, so a dim light of any frequency should eventually supply enough energy to free an electron - it would merely take longer. Neither prediction is observed. Einstein's model, in which energy arrives in packets of $hf$, explains both at once: a single photon below the threshold simply cannot free an electron, and a photon above it hands over $hf - \phi$ immediately.
